source: Woods, Patterson, Roth (2002) Can we ever escape from data overload? A cognitive systems diagnosis
finding: Data has no meaning alone. Significance depends on the observer's goals, context and the stage of problem solving. Three kinds of overload: clutter, workload bottleneck, finding significance. Hiding data, showing only 'important' items, letting the machine decide, or using statistical cues all fail.
numbers: Five design guidelines: organization before selectivity, positive selection (spotlight) over negative filters, context shown in the world, observability, conceptual spaces. No experiment numbers in the note.
quote: A little more technology, by itself, is not enough.
limits: Read through a blog summary by Fred Hebert, not the original paper. Journal version 2002 (Cognition, Technology & Work 4:22-36); a 1998 AFRL report has the same title.
agent_relevance: An impasse detector must read the output against the current goal and state, not against a fixed list of important signs. Raw log dumps to the model are the clutter failure.

source: Woods (1995) The alarm problem and directed attention in dynamic fault management
finding: Alarms fail as nuisance alarms, ambiguous messages, alarm inflation and status updates. They are densest when load is highest. Attention is directed by signals that refer to shared context. Practitioners treat uninformative alarm systems as a single master caution alarm.
numbers: Cases: nuclear rod-position counters that click faster as rods move, fixed-tile annunciators read by peripheral vision, a hue-coded icon display where faults cascade and hide changes. No sample sizes in the note.
quote: Alarms are examples of attention directing cognitive tools.
limits: Read through a blog summary by Fred Hebert, not the original paper. Original journal article is Ergonomics 38(11), DOI 10.1080/00140139508925274 (Crossref metadata seen). Case-based, no controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Our detector should flag departures from the expected pattern in context, not every anomaly. A cheap, partial signal that does not interrupt the main line of work is the design target.

source: Woods (1995) Alarm problem: cognitive activities that the alarm must support
finding: The activities named are attention focusing, attention switching, dynamic prioritization, diagnostic search, response planning and communication. Context sensitivity is called the major challenge. Variation is the norm, so compare against background and expected patterns.
numbers: Preattentive signal needs three properties: picked up in parallel, carries partial information, light enough not to interrupt.
limits: Read through a blog summary by Fred Hebert, not the original paper. This is a different slice of the same note as a02.
agent_relevance: Maps to scaffold states: the monitor step compares output to an expected pattern; a flag carries only a short reason code.

source: Woods (1994) Cognitive demands and activities in dynamic fault management: abductive reasoning and disturbance management
finding: Founding chapter. Anomaly response is framed as two intertwined lines: diagnosing the source (abduction: pick the best explanation for the findings) and managing the disturbance (keeping the process safe while diagnosis continues).
numbers: No numbers recorded. Text not opened; only the Crossref record and a search snippet confirm the title, the book (Human Factors of Alarm Design, Stanton ed., Taylor and Francis, 1994, pp 63-92).
limits: NOT OPENED. Full text not reachable (paywalled book chapter). The framing here comes from the title and the chapter record, not from reading it.
agent_relevance: Two tracks run together in our agent: a diagnosis track (hypotheses) and a containment track (keep the budget and the answer safe). The schema should not stop containment while it diagnoses.

source: Roth, Woods, Pople (1992) Cognitive simulation as a tool for cognitive task analysis
finding: A computer model of operator cognition in dynamic fault management (the Cognitive Environment Simulation, CES) was run on simulated plant emergencies to find where intention errors are likely. It is a computational model of the subfield.
numbers: No numbers recorded. Not opened.
limits: NOT OPENED. Paywalled. Known from the Crossref record (Ergonomics 35, 1992) and a search snippet. Companion records: OSTI report 1990 (DOI 10.2172/7069222) and Nuclear Engineering and Design 1992 (DOI 10.1016/0029-5493(92)90153-m).
agent_relevance: The CES idea is a precedent for testing a scaffold by running a model of the reasoner through scripted faults and checking where it forms wrong intentions.

source: Roth, Mumaw, Lewis (1994) NUREG/CR-6208 An empirical investigation of operator performance in cognitively demanding simulated emergencies
finding: Operators in nuclear plant training simulators rely on written procedures, but in several cases situation assessment and response planning dealt with parts of the emergency the procedures did not cover.
numbers: Two scenario families: Interfacing System Loss of Coolant Accident and Loss of Heat Sink (variants). Two plant sites, up to 11 crews per plant, 38 analysed cases. Westinghouse for the NRC, 1994.
limits: Only the NRC catalogue summary page was read. The 32.76 MB PDF returned HTTP 403 for both curl and the fetch tool, so detailed counts per failure type are not recorded.
agent_relevance: Procedures (our fixed rules) are enough most of the time; the cases that matter are where the rule set does not fit. The detector has to find those cases, then hand over to open reasoning.

source: Rasmussen (1983) Skills, rules and knowledge; signals, signs and symbols
finding: Three levels of behaviour: skill, rule, knowledge. Knowledge level is used when no rule fits: set a goal, plan, test by thought or trial and error. Signals, signs and symbols give three ways to read the same display. Abstraction hierarchy lets errors be traced bottom-up and reasons top-down.
numbers: Cited more than 5,000 times (per the note). 3 levels, 3 information types, 3 simplifying strategies (aggregation, abstraction, analogy).
limits: Read through a blog summary by Fred Hebert, not the original paper. Qualitative framework. The note lists no error taxonomy or experiment.
agent_relevance: The schema's rule-first, open-reasoning-on-impasse structure matches this model. An impasse is the moment a rule-level step fails and the agent drops to knowledge-level work.

source: Besnard, Greathead, Baxter (2004) When mental models go wrong: co-occurrences in dynamic, critical systems
finding: A wrong model stays in use while events match expectations, even when the cause was never found. Partial confirmation is accepted fast; contradiction needs more consistent evidence. Fixation (ignoring growing evidence) is distinguished from taking unrelated events as agreement with a wrong model.
numbers: Kegworth 1989: captain over 13,000 flying hours, first officer over 3,200, only 76 hours together on the 737-400. Throttling back the right engine stopped the vibration, so the crew kept the wrong diagnosis for about 20 minutes. 64% of pilots said the digital engine display was poor at drawing attention; 74% preferred the older style.
quote: their vision of the world is correct whenever events happen in accordance with their expectations
limits: Read through a blog summary by Fred Hebert, not the original paper. Two case studies (Kegworth, Chernobyl) plus a pilot survey. No controlled test.
agent_relevance: An output that improves after a wrong fix is a trap: a single co-occurring improvement should not close the case. Needs a check that the fix explains the original failing output (guardrails G2, G3).

source: Besnard et al. (2004) Chernobyl as fixation
finding: At Chernobyl operators held the belief that the plant could not explode and kept looking for other explanations even with graphite visible and clear signs of an explosion.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Read through a blog summary by Fred Hebert, not the original paper. Second-hand description of an accident, not a measured study.
agent_relevance: Fixation shows up as new alternative stories for the same data, not as repeating the same action. A loop detector on repeated actions alone would miss it.

source: Klein and Woods (2004) Ten challenges for making automation a team player
finding: Automation must be a teammate: mutual predictability, directability, common ground. The more adaptable an automated agent is, the less predictable it becomes. Agents should signal when they are struggling and manage attention for others.
numbers: Ten challenges, three coordination requirements. No data.
limits: Read through a blog summary by Fred Hebert, not the original paper. Position paper, year taken from background knowledge since the note omits it.
agent_relevance: Our agent should state, in a fixed format, when it hits an impasse and what it will try next, so a human or a checker can direct it.

source: Woods (2005 or later) On people and computers in joint cognitive systems at work (chapter 11, Joint Cognitive Systems: Patterns in CSE)
finding: The context gap: automation acts on a model of the world, and if the model differs from the actual situation it does the right thing for the wrong world. All procedures are brittle. People have limits too: local focus gives narrow responses and missed side effects.
numbers: After Three Mile Island operators were held responsible but could not change procedures that were incomplete or contradictory, a double bind. Two adaptations: follow rules narrowly, or build covert workarounds.
quote: No plan survives contact with a disaster-in-the-making.
limits: Read through a blog summary by Fred Hebert, not the original paper. Book chapter, no experiment. Date from the book (Hollnagel and Woods 2005/2006), not stated in the note.
agent_relevance: Every scaffold rule is brittle at its edge. The detector exists to notice the context gap: the case in which the rule's assumed world differs from the real one.

source: Cook and Long (2020) Building and revising adaptive capacity sharing for technical incident response
finding: A software company built a support cadre that joins long incidents. Three incident traits decide whether sharing works: tempo, duration, magnitude. Sharing consumes capacity and needs replenishment. Resilience depends on communication.
numbers: About a dozen incidents per week; cadre of 8 engineers and managers; auto-paging when incidents run long.
limits: Read through a blog summary by Fred Hebert, not the original paper. One case report, no controlled comparison. Applied Ergonomics.
agent_relevance: Escalate by budget rule (time or step count) instead of waiting for the stuck agent to notice it is stuck: our detector should be code-run, not self-reported (G1).

source: SNAFUcatchers (2017) STELLA report on coping with complexity
finding: Three incident cases in web operations (Apache build spreading across a fleet, Travis CI outage from a failing RabbitMQ server, Logstash slowdown). Anomalies came from interactions between components, triggered by near-normal conditions. Responders searched iteratively and abandoned hypotheses; buffers ran out; people shed low-priority goals.
numbers: 3 cases. Common reaction: 'I didn't know that it worked this way'.
limits: Read through the site's page text, first 100,000 of 135,042 characters. The report does not discuss fixation by name. Case studies of the workshop, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Multi-cause faults mean the first hypothesis can be right yet insufficient. The agent should allow several causes to be tracked, and should treat a fix that only partly works as a signal.

source: Finin and Morris (1989) Abductive reasoning in multiple fault diagnosis
finding: Compares five formal ways to build an explanation for a set of faults: binary-choice Bayesian, sequential Bayesian, causal model-based abduction, parsimonious set covering, first-order logic. Shows each on a car-troubleshooting example.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Only the catalogue page and abstract were read; the PDF is a scanned image that could not be read as text. It is a formal-model source for abductive diagnosis, which Woods's chapter builds on (not verified).
agent_relevance: Parsimonious set covering gives a code-checkable form of 'best explanation': the smallest set of causes that covers all observed symptoms. A cheap test for G3.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: a holistic framework to evaluate AI agents for autonomous clouds
finding: 48 injected-fault problems in microservice clouds, four task levels (detect, localize, root-cause, mitigate), four LLM agents. Best accuracy was 59.32%. Detection is a binary question yet only one agent got all of it right.
numbers: Overall accuracy: FLASH 59.32%, ReAct 55.93%, GPT-4 with shell 49.15%, GPT-3.5 with shell 15.25%. Mitigation: GPT-3.5 recovered 0 failures. Two no-fault problems: only GPT-4 said normal; the others reported false alarms.
limits: Four agents, one benchmark, microservice cloud only. Accuracy plateaued with more steps (GPT-3.5 gained nothing past 5 steps).
agent_relevance: False alarms on normal activity show an agent with no baseline of normal. Our detector needs a baseline of expected output before it can call something an anomaly.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: agent failure modes
finding: Agents waste steps by repeating the same call, calling non-existent APIs, and talking in circles in multi-agent mode. One agent repeated 'I apologize for the error. Here is the API call again' with the same mistake as many as 14 times in a 20-step problem. Dumping raw telemetry into context overloads the model.
numbers: Up to 14 repeats within 20 steps. ReAct, by contrast, usually fixed a bad call after reading the error.
limits: Descriptive, from trace reading; frequencies per failure type are not given beyond the example.
agent_relevance: A repeat-count rule is cheap to code and catches this stuck-in-outdated-behaviour pattern. Decompensation (budget spent, no change) is visible as a flat accuracy curve past a step count.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: self-repair from feedback saturates
finding: More steps raised accuracy up to a point, then flattened. The authors say self-repair with environment feedback saturates fast for operations problems, unlike code tasks where tests and linters keep helping.
numbers: FLASH reached its best 59.32% only at the largest step limit tested (20 steps). GPT-3.5 gained nothing beyond 5 steps.
limits: Step limit sweep on a small benchmark.
agent_relevance: Supports a hard step cap plus a switch of strategy instead of more of the same loop. Matches the schema rule that more doubt on a schedule does not help.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: evaluating AI agents across diverse real-world IT automation tasks
finding: 94 real-world scenarios in three areas. Best agents resolved 13.8% of SRE scenarios, 25.2% of CISO scenarios and 0% of FinOps scenarios.
numbers: GPT-4o diagnosis pass@1 on SRE: 13.81%; mitigation 11.43%. By difficulty, diagnosis was 36% easy, 7.73% medium, 5.0% hard; mitigation 21%, 12.27%, 0.0%. Without trace data diagnosis fell from 13.81% to 9.52% and mitigation to 2.86%. Mix: 24% easy, 24% medium, 52% hard.
limits: Run-to-run variability is large (the paper shows non-deterministic outcomes). Benchmark from one group.
agent_relevance: Hard anomalies with several causes are where agents fall to near zero, which is the region an impasse handler must cover. Observability (traces) matters: the detector needs signals to read.

source: Wang et al. (2024) RCAgent: cloud root cause analysis by autonomous agents with tool-augmented LLMs
finding: Controller agent with tools, an observation-key store, a JSON regeneration step and self-consistency voting. Stability measured as pass rate within 15 steps.
numbers: Full system: 99.38% pass rate within 15 steps, 7.93% invalid-action rate. With nucleus sampling instead of default decoding: 70.19% pass, 44.80% invalid. One ablation (probably removing the JSON regeneration step; the text is ambiguous) cut the pass rate by 33.54% and gave a 70.95% invalid rate.
limits: Production data from one company (Alibaba cloud); ablation numbers read from text, the table layout was garbled.
agent_relevance: Stability comes from code around the model (key store, regeneration, checks), not from asking the model to be careful. It supports the code-decides design.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based agents for root cause analysis
finding: A ReAct agent with retrieval tools was compared with retrieval and chain-of-thought baselines on production incidents. ReAct matched them on correctness with much less invention of facts.
numbers: Correct on about 35% for the best ReAct variant versus 39% for baselines. Hallucination rate about 4% for ReAct versus 12% for CoT and 40% for plain retrieval.
limits: Out-of-distribution internal incident set; labels by two authors on 100 sampled predictions per model; small N for each cell.
agent_relevance: Letting the agent gather evidence cut invention but did not raise accuracy. Collecting data is not diagnosis: the revise step has to decide from the gathered output.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes in three groups, built from 150 traces and applied to 1642 traces from 7 frameworks. Failure rates 41% to 86.7%. Step repetition is a named mode, as are premature termination and no or incomplete verification.
numbers: Step repetition 15.7% of failures; not recognising task completion 12.4%; disobey task specification 11.8%. Annotator agreement kappa 0.88; the LLM annotator reached 94% accuracy and kappa 0.77. One fix to a role gave +9.4% task success.
limits: Percentages differ between paper versions (v3 figure shows 11.5% for step repetition); counts are of failure modes among failed traces, not of runs.
agent_relevance: Names and measures our own three failure patterns: stuck in repetition is code-detectable, and no-verification is the G3 gap.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which agent causes task failures and when? Who&When
finding: Anomaly localisation inside an agent run is itself hard. Best automatic method names the guilty agent 53.5% of the time but the decisive step only 14.2%.
numbers: 127 LLM multi-agent systems in the dataset. Agent-level 53.5%, step-level 14.2%; some methods below random; o1 and R1 not usable in practice.
limits: Failure logs from multi-agent systems, not human operators.
agent_relevance: A judge model cannot reliably find where a run went wrong. Step location should come from code (diffs, counters, first failing output), as G2 says.

source: Woods and Hollnagel (2006) Joint Cognitive Systems: Patterns in Cognitive Systems Engineering
finding: Book that states the pattern language of CSE. Woods's three failure patterns in anomaly response (decompensation, working at cross purposes, getting stuck in outdated behaviour) belong to this literature.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: NOT OPENED. The fetch returned 403. The three-pattern list comes from the project note SUBFIELDS.md and background knowledge, not from reading the chapter.
agent_relevance: These are the labels for our impasse classes: budget burnt with no change, sub-attempts undoing each other, repeating a dead rule.

source: De Keyser and Woods (1990) Fixation errors: failures to revise situation assessment in dynamic and risky systems
finding: Founding paper on fixation: operators keep an earlier assessment while evidence against it grows. Named here for the record.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: NOT OPENED. Search budget ran out before it could be found; no URL verified. Title and year from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Fixation is the failure our revise operator must break. Needs the real paper before any claim about rates.

source: Cook and Woods (1996) Adapting to new technology in the operating room
finding: Field study of anaesthesia and surgery teams adapting to a new cardiac monitor, with workarounds ('tailoring'). Recorded as a lead to open.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: NOT OPENED. No verified URL; details from background knowledge only.
agent_relevance: Lead for angle B. Shows that users adapt tools to cope; our agent may need the same room to adapt its rules.

source: Search budget note: foundational Woods experiments not reachable
finding: Of the founding sources (Woods 1994 chapter, Roth et al. 1992, NUREG/CR-6208 PDF, De Keyser and Woods 1990) none could be read as full text. Reached only through catalogue pages and third-party summaries.
numbers: 0 of 4 founding primary texts opened in full.
limits: Web search quota was used up, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned rate limits, DTIC, OSTI and NRC PDFs returned 403 or refused connections.
agent_relevance: Do not build rules on exact rates from this file for the founding studies; re-open them once access exists.
